turns: Hey Sam, can we push Monday's project call to Tuesday? The client still needs a day to look at the draft.
Tuesday works for me. Do we still need the full hour?
Honestly, no. Let's keep it to thirty minutes. We only need to land on the next step.
Should I send the slides over beforehand?
That'd be great. If they go out Monday afternoon, people can actually read them instead of watching you read them.
Fair enough. I'll update the invite and put the new goal in the subject line.
Perfect. The time's changing — the goal isn't.
Quick update on the site. Home page is done, and we're testing the contact form now.
Are we still good for Friday?
Mostly. We're waiting on the final product photos. Without them I can check the layout, but I can't finish the product page.
What do you need from me?
Could you chase the design team and get the photos by tomorrow morning?
Thanks. If they land on time, Friday still holds. I'll shout if anything shifts.
Could you make the report a bit shorter?
Sure. When you say shorter — fewer pages, or less detail?
Fewer pages. The managers want something they can skim before the discussion.
Keep the two that carry the argument. Put the extra tables in a separate file.
Okay, so the main report is the key findings plus two examples, and everything else lives next to it.
It is. I'll send the short version and keep the rest one click away.
I've looked at the vendor proposal, and I'd go with the second option. It's cheaper and it starts sooner.
I hear you on the price. My worry is support — the second vendor has one person covering our whole region.
That's a fair point. I hadn't weighted response time as heavily as cost.
So we're not really disagreeing about the goal. We're weighing different risks.
Right. What if we ask both vendors for their escalation numbers and a named backup?
I'd be happy with that. If the second vendor can show real cover, the savings are hard to argue with.
Then let's not decide today. I'll send both of them the same two questions and we can compare answers on Thursday.
Works for me. And thanks for not treating my objection as an attack.
Bad news first — the payment integration is slower than we thought. As things stand, Friday isn't happening.
The happy path works. Error handling and refunds are what's eating the time. I'd need until Wednesday for all three.
Two, really. We ship Friday with payments and refunds, and error handling follows the week after — or we hold everything to Wednesday and launch once.
What breaks if error handling comes later?
A failed payment shows a generic message instead of telling the customer what to do. It's ugly, but it doesn't lose money.
Then ship Friday and put a note in the release saying what's missing. I'd rather be honest about the gap than silent about it.
Good. I'll write the known-issues list today so nobody's surprised.
So I ran the numbers past Hannah, and she said, “interesting — let's revisit this next quarter.”
It's not a yes either. She used to say “let's do it” when she meant it.
What did she do with the last proposal she pushed back on?
She asked for more detail, twice, and then it quietly disappeared.
Then “revisit next quarter” might mean she doesn't want to say no in front of the team.
That's my read too. But it's still a read. I could be wrong.
I'll ask her directly what would have to change for it to happen this quarter. If she can name conditions, it's alive. If she goes vague again, I'll treat it as a no and stop spending time on it.
That's better than guessing in either direction.
Okay, hear me out. A subscription box for specialty coffee — recurring revenue, loyal customers, and the margins look fantastic on paper.
On paper. What's the churn assumption?
Four percent a month, which is what the article I read used.
Right. And where did that article get it from?
…I don't actually know. It was a summary of a summary.
That's the thing. The idea is attractive, and attractive ideas generate numbers that flatter them. What would convince you it's real?
Pre-orders from people who don't know me.
That's a start. And what would convince you it isn't?
If fifty strangers won't commit ten pounds before they've tasted anything, the margin story collapses — we'd be a shop with extra steps.
Then let's not build the business yet. Let's build the test. Two weeks, fifty strangers, one landing page.
Deal. Though I'm noticing I want the answer to be yes.
Good that you said it out loud. That's exactly the feeling that ruins a decision.
Our return rate is eleven percent. Legal wants to know if that's a problem.
Eleven percent of what, and compared with whom?
Of units shipped this quarter. Last year it was eight.
Okay, so the honest sentence is “up three points year on year”, not “eleven percent”. Eleven on its own doesn't mean anything.
The category average is around nine, I think.
“I think” — can we source that? Because if it's nine, we're two points above the market and that's a real conversation. If it's thirteen, we're fine and Legal can relax.
And the mix changed. We launched two new products this quarter.
Then the aggregate is hiding the answer. Split old products from new. If the old ones are still at eight, the problem is a design issue in the new line, not a company-wide slide.
That's a much smaller question to investigate.
Smaller and answerable. Also say what the denominator did — if shipments jumped, eleven percent might be the same number of returns as before.
I'll come back with the split and the source for the category figure. No more bare numbers.
Right, nobody's objected, so we're agreed. I'll send it out as decided.
Can I slow this down for a second? Nobody's objected out loud, but that's not the same as everybody agreeing.
Three people have said nothing at all. Mei's been looking at her laptop since the slide changed, and Tomas raised this concern last month and got talked round.
So you think there's disagreement we haven't heard?
I think there's disagreement that's expensive to raise after we've announced it. Quiet is cheap now and costly later.
One round, thirty seconds each, and the question isn't “any objections?” — it's “what would make this fail?” That's easier to answer honestly.
And if someone names a real risk?
Then we've spent five minutes now instead of a month in November. Mei — you've been quiet. What would make this fail?
Honestly? The handover. Nobody's written down what happens when the current team leaves.
…Okay. Not agreed yet. Let's fix that first.
Hi — sorry to bother you. A parcel was delivered to my flat by mistake this morning, and I think it's yours.
Oh! That'll be the lamp I ordered. I've been watching the door all day.
It's just here in the hall. I didn't want to leave it outside in case it went missing.
That was kind of you. I'd have been annoyed with the driver, not with you.
Well, the label's tiny. I only checked because the name looked familiar.
Do you want a hand carrying it? It says fragile.
Actually, yes — it's heavier than it looks.
Right, one, two… there we go. Thanks again. If a parcel of yours ever lands here, I'll bring it round straight away.
Much appreciated. And if you ever need anything collected while you're away, just knock.
So, a few of us are doing a climbing session on Saturday morning. You should come.
Indoor wall, big mats, ropes everywhere. Nobody's going anywhere near a cliff.
I'll be honest — I'm not sure I'd be any good at it.
Nobody is on their first time. That's kind of the point.
Whatever you can move in. Shoes are at the place. There's a café too, so if you hate it after twenty minutes, you can sit and judge the rest of us.
That's a very good offer. Okay, I'll come.
Brilliant. I'll send you the time and where to meet.
Thanks for asking, actually. I'd never have suggested it myself.
That's usually how these things start.
The fourteen twenty to York is cancelled. The board says replacement bus, but no platform.
How long do we have before the wedding starts?
Ceremony's at five. Bus is three hours if traffic's kind.
Then we'd arrive at five-ish, which is not really an option.
There's a train at fifteen ten from the next station. Two stops by tram, about eighteen minutes.
Not automatically. But this cancellation's the operator's fault, so I'll ask for an endorsement rather than buying new ones.
Then we buy two new singles and claim the original back later — I'll photograph the board first, because that's the evidence.
You get the tram times and keep the bags moving. I'll do the queue. If I'm not back in twelve minutes, leave without me and I'll get the next one.
I'd rather we both make the ceremony, but fine — twelve minutes.
Evening. Have you eaten with us before?
Not yet. A friend recommended the lamb, but I can't tell what the sauce is from the menu.
It's a pomegranate and walnut sauce — sour, a bit sweet, quite rich. It's not spicy.
That sounds good. Is it a large portion? I don't want to overorder.
It's generous. Two people often share it with bread and one side.
Then I'll have the lamb and the aubergine. Could I ask for the sauce on the side, just so I can taste it first?
Of course. That's a sensible way to try something new.
And what do you drink with it?
The house red stands up to it well. If you'd rather not, the mint and lime is refreshing against the richness.
Mint and lime, please. Thank you for explaining rather than just saying it's nice.
Anytime. Describing it is my job; deciding is yours.
I thought the ending was hopeful, actually. She goes back to the town and starts over.
See, I read it the other way. I think she goes back because there's nowhere else to go.
That makes sense. The last scene is quiet enough to hold both of those.
Right. And she smiles when she sees the house — but we never see what happens on Tuesday.
Maybe that's why I liked it. It lets you sit with the not-knowing.
I'm still not convinced I liked the ending. But I enjoyed arguing about it.
That's the bit I always forget — you don't have to like a thing to have a good conversation about it.
Exactly. Though if they'd shown one more scene, I'd probably have changed my mind.
Or found a new reason to disagree.
Did you see this? Coffee protects against memory loss. Should I be drinking four a day?
What does the article actually say they did?
Hmm. They followed thirty thousand people for ten years and asked how much coffee they drank.
So they observed people, they didn't assign coffee. That's a cohort study, not a trial.
It matters a lot. People who drink coffee differ from people who don't — in sleep, in income, in whether they have a job with fixed breaks. Any of those could carry the effect.
So the honest headline would be…
Coffee drinkers in this study showed slower decline. Which might mean coffee helps, or might mean something about coffee drinkers helps.
Nothing here supports four a day. The study doesn't test doses, and more of a thing that's merely associated isn't a prescription.
A randomised trial with a real control group, or several cohorts in different countries showing the same size of effect. One headline isn't either.
Can I just tell you about my week without you solving it?
Yes. I'll shut up and listen. Go on.
I got passed over for the lead role on the migration. Again. And the worst part is I saw it coming and said nothing.
That's a horrible feeling — seeing it and not saying anything.
Right. And then Mum rang and asked when I'd be promoted, like it's a timetable.
So it's not only the decision, it's having to explain it to her too.
Exactly. …Actually, that's the part that got me.
Do you want me to keep listening, or do you want thoughts?
Okay. One thought: asking at the start like you did — that worked. It told me what you needed instead of leaving me to guess.
It shows. And for what it's worth, I'd have said something clumsy about updating your CV, which wasn't the point at all.
I ordered it at eleven at night and it was on my doorstep by seven. That's remarkable, whatever else you say.
It is remarkable. It's also not magic — somebody drove it at four in the morning.
Sure, and they're paid for that.
Are they paid for the waiting? The shift that ends whenever the last drop finishes? That's the part that doesn't show up in the price.
So your argument is we should be less convenient?
No — my argument is that convenience is a transfer, not a creation. The time saved has to come from somewhere, and usually it comes from whoever has least power to refuse.
That's harder to dismiss than I expected. Though I'd say the customer gains too. A parent who can't shop at three in the afternoon genuinely benefits.
Agreed, and that's a real benefit — I'm not proposing we go back. I'm asking whether we know the full cost, because a price that hides part of itself gets chosen too often.
What would make the cost visible?
Delivery windows that don't run overnight, and honest labelling about shift length. Then people can still choose speed — but they'd be choosing it, not inheriting it.
Hi — this is the third time I've written about the boiler. It cut out again last night, around two.
I'm sorry, I had it marked as done after the engineer visited on the fourth.
He came, looked at it and said the part would be ordered. Nothing's happened since, and I've got the message log if that helps.
Send it over. Can I ask what it's doing exactly?
It fires up, runs about ten minutes, then stops and shows an error light. The heating comes back if I reset it, but not overnight.
That sounds like the part he ordered. It should have been fitted last week.
I understand that. What I need is a date, because I've got a baby in the flat and the nights are getting cold.
Fair. I'll call the supplier now and come back to you before five with a fitted date — not another visit date.
Thank you. If it slips again, I'll write to the housing officer. Not as a threat, just so there's a record either way.
That's reasonable. You should have had this fixed on the first call.
So the whole group's doing a weekend in the mountains — leaving Friday night, back Sunday. You in?
I want to be, and I'm going to say no this time.
Yeah, nothing's wrong. It's just that I've done three weekends in a row and I'm running on empty. If I come, I'll be the person sitting in the corner at nine.
That's fair. Honestly, half of them will be in bed by ten.
What I don't want is for this to turn into me not being invited.
That won't happen. Though you should know Priya's already organising something in two weeks, and it's the quiet kind — dinner, one long table.
That one I'd genuinely like. Can I say yes to that now and skip this one without it being weird?
Completely normal. People come to some things and not others.
Then that's what I'll do. Tell them I'm sorry to miss it, and that I want photos.
You'll get four hundred photos and a running commentary whether you want them or not.
Good afternoon. What can I help you with?
Hi. My flight to Lisbon was cancelled and I've been told to come here. I'm not sure what happens to my bag.
Let me look. Can I see the boarding pass and the bag tag?
Here you go. The tag's on the back of the pass.
Thanks. Right — the bag went on the earlier flight, so it's already in Lisbon. It'll be held at the desk there.
Oh, that's easier than I thought. And me?
There's one seat on the eighteen forty, or three on the morning flight. Neither costs anything, since this is our cancellation.
The eighteen forty, please. I'd rather get there tonight.
Done. Here's your new pass, and this sheet has the bag desk location and the number to call if it isn't there.
One more thing — is the hotel near the airport? I get in late.
It's the one at the terminal, about four minutes on foot. I've put the reference on the same sheet.
Perfect. That's much clearer than I expected.
Table for two? Right this way. Have you eaten here before?
First time. I should mention — I can't have shellfish. Not a preference, it's an allergy.
Thank you for saying so. Let me flag that to the kitchen now, before you order.
I appreciate that. Is it a kitchen where things share surfaces?
It's a small kitchen, so I'll ask them to note cross-contact. The grilled sea bass is safe, and so are the two pastas made without seafood stock.
That's helpful. I'll take the sea bass. And could I check — does the bread come with anything on it?
Salted butter, no shellfish. I'll ask for it plain if you'd prefer.
Butter's fine. One more thing: if there's any doubt about a dish later, I'd rather it came back than I guessed.
Understood. I'll tell the server directly, and we won't bring anything to the table that hasn't been checked.
Perfect. That's the first time I've not had to explain it three times.
You shouldn't have to. Say it once and we'll hold it.
More than worth it. The second song had the whole room quiet, which I wasn't expecting at a place that size.
I kept thinking about the drummer. She barely looked at her kit the entire set.
Right? And the singer introduced one song by saying it was written on a night bus, and you could hear that.
It had that tired, half-awake feeling. Not sad exactly — more like watching a city through a window at midnight.
That's a good way to put it. I'd have just said I liked it.
You liked the encore more than I did, though. You were on your feet.
I was! It's the only one I'd want to hear again immediately.
Same. So, one song each — what are you taking home?
The bus one. I'll probably annoy you with it for a week.
I've had three coffees today and I'm still exhausted. Isn't caffeine supposed to fix this?
It doesn't fix it — it hides it. Caffeine blocks the receptors that adenosine docks onto, so you stop feeling the sleep pressure building up.
Exactly. It keeps accumulating. When the caffeine wears off, all of it arrives at once, which is why the crash feels worse than the tiredness did.
So the third cup is doing less than the first.

Less, and later. Caffeine's half-life is around five hours for most people, so an afternoon cup is still half there at bedtime. It won't stop you falling asleep, but it can reduce the deep sleep you get.
Which means I wake up tired, drink more, and it gets worse.
That's the loop. The useful test isn't how you feel at four in the afternoon — it's whether you'd feel the same without the coffee.
How would I even check that?
Cut it after eleven in the morning for two weeks and see. If your sleep improves and the afternoons get easier, the coffee was borrowing energy rather than making it.
Borrowing. That's an uncomfortable way to describe my entire routine.
It's the mechanism, though. Nothing's being created; something's being moved to later.
You've read the message Mum sent, then.
I have. And before you start — I'm not going to tell you what to do with your own life.
She did. And I think she's wrong about the deadline she's set you. That doesn't mean she's wrong to be worried.
Those feel like the same thing to her.
They might. But you can hold both. You can say: I hear that you're frightened, and I'm not making this decision by the date you want.
I've tried something like that. It comes out sounding cold.
Then put the warmth first and the boundary second, in the same sentence. Not two messages a day apart — she'll read the gap as a withdrawal.
So something like… I know this scares you, and I'm not going to rush it, and I do want you to know what I decide.
That's nearly perfect. You've told her she's not being cut out, which is the actual fear underneath the deadline.
Then repeat the same sentence. Consistency isn't stubbornness — it's the only thing that eventually lowers the temperature.
I'd rather be wrong and calm than right and exhausted.
You can be both. That's the part nobody tells you.
I've got my morning down to eleven minutes. Shower, coffee, out the door. It's extremely efficient.
And what have you gained with the twenty minutes you saved?
…I've no idea. I usually spend it scrolling in the car park.
So the efficiency went straight back into the machine.
Is it? Efficiency is brilliant at answering “how fast”, and useless at answering “what for”. Once you get good at the first question, you stop asking the second.
But you can't be wasteful with time either.
Agreed — I'm not arguing for dawdling. I'm arguing that the saving should land somewhere you chose. Eleven minutes is fine if the extra twenty goes to something you'd defend.
A walk without your phone. Breakfast sitting down. Ten minutes of not being productive, which turns out to be when people have ideas.
So the test isn't whether I'm fast. It's whether I know what the speed is for.
And whether you'd still choose it if you had to say out loud what it buys.
Did you see the headline about the new bus lane?
I did. "City removes parking for a lane nobody uses."
That's not quite what the report said. The lane opens next month.
So the nobody-uses part is a guess.
It's worse than a guess. It's the number of cars counted before the lane existed.
Right. So they measured an empty road and called it evidence.
The report does say parking losses are real for two shops on that street.
That part matters. I just don't like it being sold as a verdict.
Agreed. Hold both: some shops lose, and the lane hasn't been tested yet.
You look tired. Are you sleeping at all?
Not much. Work's been strange and my head won't switch off.
Do you want advice, or do you want me to just listen for a bit?
Honestly? Listen. Everyone keeps telling me to exercise.
A walk does help me, but I'm not going to pretend it fixes your week.
That's the thing. It helps for an hour. Then it's the same.
So what would actually help tonight?
Eating something that isn't toast, probably. And not being told I need a routine.
I can do dinner. I can't do your routine.
My phone asked if I want to share location with the app for a better experience.
What does a better experience mean?
No idea. It's the same experience with more data.
I did, and now it asks every single time I open it.
That's the design. Friction is a nudge.
So they make the private option annoying.
Exactly. Not blocked, just slightly more work than saying yes.
I keep saying yes at night. I'm too tired to read anything.
Then change the default once, when you're not tired.
That's the only advice that has ever worked on me.
I've been rereading the same chapter for an hour and I still can't explain it.
Rereading feels productive because the page looks familiar.
Familiar isn't the same as known.
Right. Try closing the book and writing what you remember. It will feel awful.
It does feel awful. I got about a third of it.
That third is real. The other two thirds were the page doing the work.
So the comfortable version was the one wasting my time.
Not wasting. It just doesn't test anything.
How often should I do the painful version?
Short and often. Ten minutes beats an hour once a week.
I did that thing where you add up your subscriptions.
Eleven a month on a film service I stopped watching in March.
Eleven times eight months is eighty-eight. For nothing.
I tried. The cancel button is behind three pages and one survey.
So is the free trial that needs a card.
I cancelled four last night. Took twenty minutes.
And how much did you save?
About thirty a month. I nearly spent it immediately.
The building finally got the separate bins.
And half of it is in the wrong one already.
Give people a week. Nobody grew up sorting this.
The signs are tiny. You need to stand right in front of them.
That's fixable. Bigger labels, one picture each.
What actually gets me is the food waste. It smells and nobody takes it down.
So we take it down on the same day each week. Tuesday, before the shop.
Mine, then yours. And if one of us forgets, the other says so without a speech.
So, the flat. Great light, terrible kitchen.
The kitchen is small, but it works. I cooked in worse for years.
There's no window in the bathroom.
That one I can't fix. Mould will find it eventually.
And the street is loud until about eleven.
Loud at night I can handle. Loud at six in the morning I can't.
Let's check tomorrow at six, then, before we decide.
That's the most sensible thing anyone has said all week.
If it's quiet at six, I'd take it. The kitchen I can live with.
Same. But I want to hear the six o'clock version first.
We lost by two and everyone's talking about the referee.
The referee was bad. We were also bad for twenty minutes.
Right after half time. We stopped moving and let them walk through.
That's when the second goal came.
So we can fix that. We can't fix the referee.
They never do. But if we blame the whistle, we practice nothing this week.
Fair. So what do we actually work on?
Movement without the ball. Ten minutes at the start of every session.
Mum's decided the whole family is coming for the holiday. All of us.
Including the cousin you haven't spoken to since the wedding?
Especially him. She thinks a table fixes things.
It fixes her worry for one afternoon.
I want to see her. I don't want to pretend nothing happened.
Then say that. Two sentences, no accusation.
I'll come for you. I'm not ready to pretend with him.
That's honest and it gives her something to work with.
Probably. Then she'll plan the seating.
They offered me the lead role on the new project.
That's the one you wanted six months ago.
It is. And I'm probably going to say no.
Because it starts in the same month as the thing I already promised.
Badly, yes. The last time I did both, I delivered neither properly.
So what's the actual reason you'd give them?
That I can't give it the time it needs, and I'd rather say that now than in month two.
A no with a reason is easier to hear than a slow yes that collapses.
They're removing the benches on the square.
The three near the fountain. Apparently people loiter.
People sit down. That's what a square is for.
The shop owners say it hurts business.
Did anyone ask the people who sit there?
The consultation had eleven responses. All from the street with the shops.
So the sample decided the square.
There's a proposal to replace them with a planter edge. Low, narrow.
That's a bench you can't rest on. Design as a polite refusal.
Exactly. It looks like seating and works as a barrier.
